idiom_name: using-clauses resolved by given instances (term inference at the call site)
implementation_notes: Context parameters absorb the pattern into the language: a method declares (using Config), callers omit the argument, and the compiler performs term inference - it fills in the canonical given value of that type visible at the call site. The Scala documentation motivates exactly this problem (passing the config into every method is tedious and makes the program harder to read, because each call site has to ignore an argument it does not use) and offers both directions: a single canonical given for the type, or explicit provision f(x)(using cfg) for one call. Shadowing is lexical: an inner given wins for calls written in its scope.
code_sketch:
case class Config(port: Int, baseUrl: String)

def renderWebsite(path: String)(using Config): String =
  renderWidget(List("cart"))

given Config = Config(8080, "docs.scala-lang.org")   // the ambient provider
pitfalls: Resolution is lexical, not dynamic: the provider must be in scope where the call is written, so a value cannot be rebound per subtree the way a provider node can.
Two givens of the same type in scope make the call ambiguous - resolution then depends on which import shadows which, which is hard to reason about from the call site.
Adding a new given import can change which value an existing call uses without touching that call, so provisioning is fragile under refactoring.

variants.name: Scala 2 implicit parameters and values
variants.implementation_notes: The Scala 2 form of the same mechanism: an implicit val provides the canonical value and an implicit parameter list (implicit config: Config) consumes it, with the name of the parameter still mandatory. It remains the realization for 2.13 codebases and for libraries that support both, and it carries the wider Scala 2 implicit search - one keyword covers parameters, conversions and extension-style classes - which makes accidental capture easier than with the Scala 3 split into given/using and Conversion.
variants.code_sketch:
implicit val config: Config = Config(8080, "docs.scala-lang.org")

def renderWidget(items: List[String])(implicit config: Config): String = ???

renderWidget(List("cart"))   // config supplied implicitly
pitfalls: Which implicit is chosen depends on scope and import order, so 'which config is in effect' is decided at compile time by imports rather than by the call site.
The same keyword also declares implicit conversions, so a stray implicit can change resolution or insert a conversion unnoticed.
Implicit parameters must be named and can be shadowed by an unrelated implicit of the same type, producing confusing ambiguity errors.

variants.name: ZIO environment (R type) with ZLayer provisioning
variants.idiom_name: ZIO[R, E, A] environment + ZIO.service[A] + provide/provideLayer
variants.implementation_notes: In effect systems the context is a type parameter: ZIO[R, E, A] records that the effect requires an environment R, effect bodies pull what they need with ZIO.service[A] instead of taking parameters, and the edge of the program eliminates R with provide/provideLayer once the layer stack is assembled. Nested provide calls rebind the environment for a subgraph, giving the same scoped-override semantics as a nested provider, with the difference that the requirement is visible in every signature until it is satisfied.
pitfalls: R grows with every service, so combining effects produces wide intersection types unless a module or facade hides the set behind one requirement.
A missing or misplaced provide leaves the effect un-runnable and surfaces as a layer error at run time rather than as a compile error.
The effect signature is the documentation: widening R for convenience (requiring more than the body uses) spreads the requirement through the whole program.
